newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Bundesbank, Bonn act to counter dollar surge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bundesbank, Bonn act to counter dollar surge.

text.p: Germany on Wednesday acted to counter a sharp rise in the U.S. dollar against the mark, knocking down a report from U.S. news agency MNSI which said Germany was keen to see a further rise in the dollar.

Chief Bundesbank spokesman Manfred Koerber, in an official statement from the central bank, said the Bundesbank continued to support a statement made by the Group of Seven industrial nations at a meeting in Berlin this weekend.
"That statement said the dollar has been corrected, and it was made at a rate of 1.65 marks," he said. The dollar surged to about 1.69 marks on Wednesday morning after the MNSI report.
The dollar fell to as low as 1.6750 marks in an immediate response to the Bundesbank statement on Wednesday morning. It was trading at 1.6780 marks.
"The opinion expressed in the MNSI report does not exist within the Bundesbank," Koerber said.
"The Bundesbank firmly backs the Berlin statement. The Bundesbank is definitively not of the opinion that the dollar should rise further," he added.

This weekend, finance ministers and central bank governors of the G7 nations said that the misalignment in the dollar when it fell to a record low in 1995 had been corrected and that they did not want to see excessive market volatility.

Only two years ago the G7 -- which groups Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- acted to bring the dollar back from record lows against the mark and yen by calling for its orderly reversal.
Its rise has been particularly good for Europe, boosting exports and lifting growth as countries rush to cut budget deficits in time for the launch of a single currency in 1999.

It has also helped the United States, keeping import prices low and helping to maintain low inflation in its own economy, though U.S. carmakers are beginning to squeal about the effect of the dollar's rise on their exports.
But the dollar's overall strength has forced sharp losses for the Japanese yen, which is starting to look risky for its financial system.

Market News Service, quoting sources close to the German finance ministry and central bank, said Germany would nonetheless welcome a further dollar rise to a range of 1.70 to 1.75 marks over time to boost its economy.
The agency did not name the sources.
Earlier on Tuesday, the dollar had been knocked slightly lower after the German finance ministry said it had nothing to add to the G7 statement.

A second Bundesbank spokesman also said earlier in answer to Reuter enquiries, "We can see no substance to this report. The Bundesbank, like the Finance Ministry, has nothing to add to the G7 statement made in Berlin."

The Bundesbank's Koerber also noted in his statement that Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin had again repeated his view that although the U.S. was interested in a strong dollar, the dollar had now been strong for some time.

Rubin's statement, first made in this formulation on Friday, was seen by financial markets as a subtle change in the U.S. position. The administration had in the past repeatedly called for a strong dollar.
